branches:general.title: Branches
branches:general.body:
This page answers: which git branches am I translating, how far along is each, and is one ready to merge? Catalogue files are never copied, checked out or committed by this page; they travel through git as usual.

What a branch is here:
• Tracking a branch gives it its own state and scores under state/branches/<name>/. That is where translation provenance (model, provider, status, scores) is recorded while you work on it.
• The strings of a branch are read straight from git (git archive of the catalogue directory at the branch tip). Your working tree is not touched.
• main is the project's default source branch. 'Use main state' makes main the default again.

Status badges:
• default – the main branch.
• in progress – the branch adds or changes source strings that are not yet translated in every target locale, or it has conflicts.
• ready to merge – every added or changed string is translated and there are no conflicts.
• in sync – the branch has no source changes compared with its base.
• merged / archived – finished; the row is dimmed. Unarchive brings it back.
• no git data – the branch name or its base was not found in git (fetch it, or check the name).

Coverage: per target locale, the share of the branch's source strings with a current translation. A string without branch state falls back to main's state. Green is 80% or more, amber 40% or more, red below.

Row buttons:
• Open editor – makes the branch active and opens the editor.
• Translate → – opens Operations for that branch. Long runs go through the taskqueue; the CLI equivalent is 'llm-localizator translate --branch <name>'.
• Review / Merge → – shows the merge preview below the list.
• Archive – hides a branch from active work without deleting anything.
• Delete – forgets the branch and removes its state and scores. Permanent; asks for confirmation.

Active branch: only a default. A request or CLI call with an explicit branch always wins. Filter narrows the list by name.

branches:track.title: Branches: Track a branch
branches:track.body:
What this does:
Registers a git branch so its translation state and scores are kept apart from main. Tracking only records the branch; it does not translate anything, commit, fetch or write to your catalogues.

Fields:
• Branch name – letters, digits, '.', '_', '-' and '/'. It should already exist in the repository; if git does not know it the row shows 'no git data'.
• Base branch – the branch your work started from (usually main). New, changed and removed source strings are measured against it, and 'ready to merge' means every added or changed string is translated.
• Auto-translate new strings – stored on the branch as a preference (auto_translate, default on). It is informational today: nothing runs automatically, neither on Sync nor on save. Start translation yourself from the row's Translate button, Operations or the CLI (llm-localizator translate --branch <name>).

What tracking creates:
• state/branches/<name>/ with the branch's own translation provenance and scores, so work on a feature branch never disturbs main's records.
• A tracking date. Tracking again keeps the original date. The date matters when merging: a main entry written before tracking can be taken over, one written after is treated as a possible conflict.

After tracking:
• Open the branch row to see per-locale coverage, make it the active branch for the editor, or review the merge preview when you are done.

branches:sync.title: Branches: Sync from git
branches:sync.body:
What this does:
Shows what git currently reports, without changing anything.

• The first block is 'git status --porcelain': files changed in the working tree.
• Then one line per tracked branch: short commit, strings added (+), changed (~) and removed (-) against its base.
• git fetch (network) appears only when the repository has a remote. It runs 'git fetch --all --prune' and is the only action here that uses the network.

Sync never commits and never edits catalogues. After a fetch the list refreshes so new remote branches and commits are picked up.

branches:merge.title: Branches: Merge preview
branches:merge.body:
What this does:
Moves translation provenance from a branch's state into main's state. Catalogue text is merged by git, not here.

How each entry is classified (three-way, using the date the branch was tracked):
• New – main has no entry for the key. Applied automatically.
• Take – main's entry is older than the tracking date and is not a human or other trusted edit of the same source text. Applied automatically.
• Conflict – anything else, for example main changed the key after tracking, or main holds a human-verified translation. Never applied automatically.
• Identical entries are hidden.

Resolving conflicts: for every conflict choose Take branch (replace main's entry) or Keep main (leave it untouched). Merge to main stays disabled until every conflict has a choice.

After merging: the branch's scores are copied too, the branch is marked merged and, if it was active, main becomes active again.

Download diff saves the source changes and state rows as JSON for review or audit.

settings:llm.title: Settings: Locale → provider & model
settings:llm.body:
What this card does:
Chooses which provider and model translate, and which judge scores, each language. The 'default' row is the fallback for every locale not listed explicitly.

Columns:
• Locale – the language (or default).
• Provider – a provider defined in the card above.
• Model – the exact model tag, for example aya-expanse:8b.
• Role – Translator (only produces translations), Judge (only scores with LQS) or Both.

Saving:
• Changes are written to [locales.models] and [locales.roles]. Because model swaps change quality silently, saving a new model asks you to confirm (ADR-12). Check experiments/quality_bakeoff/REPORT.md or the Model evaluation page first, and always compare against the model currently in use.
• Roles are described by ADR-21 and judge scoring by ADR-20.

Related:
• Quality scoring (the card below) sets the score threshold below which a string is flagged.

settings:locales.title: Settings: Target locales
settings:locales.body:
What this tab does:
Lists every language the project translates into and how each one is treated.

Priority:
• ASAP – processed first in every pipeline run and highlighted on Progress.
• Normal – standard priority.
• Frozen – left out of automatic runs and out of totals, but still editable in the editor.

Columns and actions:
• Coverage – the share of source strings with a current translation.
• Model override – replaces the provider and model for this locale only. Changing models is an ADR-12 decision; run a bakeoff first.
• + Add locale – registers a new target language (ADR-47). Any valid language code is accepted; the profile of known languages adds script direction and punctuation rules (ADR-49).
• Fallback – the locale whose text is used when a string has no translation yet.
• ✕ – removes the locale from the targets after confirmation. Catalogue files are kept.

Tip:
• Freeze a locale while a translator reworks it so automated runs do not overwrite their work.

settings:project.title: Settings: Project options
settings:project.body:
What this tab does:
Project-level facts that tell the engine how to read and write your message files. Changes apply to every operation.

Project identity:
• Project name – the label shown in headings and the project list.
• Source locale – the language developers write strings in. It must not also be a target locale.

Catalogue:
• Format – json-nested, json-flat, yaml, po, arb or android-xml.
• Path template – where files live, with {locale} and {namespace} placeholders, for example messages/{locale}/{namespace}.json.
• Skip keys – comma-separated keys or patterns to ignore entirely (identifiers that should never be translated).

Saving:
• Save project settings rewrites .llm-localize.toml. The file is validated by loading it before it replaces the old one, so a bad value leaves the config unchanged.

Caveat:
• Pointing at the wrong format or path makes the project look empty. Run the Guided setup or Dashboard afterwards to confirm the key counts.

settings:web.title: Settings: Web server
settings:web.body:
What this tab does:
Shows how this review server is exposed and protects its writes.

• Bind address and Port – read-only. The server is locked to 127.0.0.1 (ADR-33, ADR-45): it only accepts connections from this computer.
• Session token – the startup token that must be sent as the X-LLM-Token header on every request that changes data. The field stays empty; press Regenerate to create a new token, which is shown once. Older tokens stop working and the page and scripts must use the new one.
• Allow cross-origin overlay edits – turns on overlay_edit so the translator overlay inside your own running app can save edits back to this server. Leave it off unless you use the overlay.
• Save web settings – stores the overlay choice.

Trust boundary:
• Signed-in users are identified by their session cookie; the token is for scripts and local tooling and acts as Admin. Keep it private.

settings:places.title: Settings: Places
settings:places.body:
What this card does:
Lists the text places the project translates and the policy for each (ADR-104). A place is a catalogue namespace or a namespace:key pattern; the most specific pattern wins.

• auto: translated like any other text.
• request: left alone unless you name the key explicitly, so nothing is translated by accident.
• review: translated, then queued for a human to check.
• never: skipped everywhere (translate, improve, rescore, status).

Save writes the [places] table in .llm-localize.toml, exactly like the places command on the CLI. Remove deletes the explicit rule so the place falls back to the default. Changing a policy never deletes existing translations.

settings:permissions.title: Settings: Permissions
settings:permissions.body:
What this tab does:
A matrix of which role may run which operation: Admin, Supervisor, Translator and Developer (ADR-39, ADR-58).

• Admin always has every permission; its column is locked.
• Translators can never run translate; that cell is locked off. Translators can still edit the strings of their assigned languages in the editor.
• Unchecking an operation removes the matching button from that role's pages and makes the server refuse the call.
• Defaults come from the built-in matrix (ops/permissions.py): translate, improve, review and rescore for Admin and Supervisor; scan, discover, doctor and push-strings for Admin and Developer; export, validate and status for everyone.

Where roles are assigned:
• Manage people on Users & roles. Language chips, not this matrix, decide which locales a person can touch.

Caveat:
• Hiding a button is a convenience; the server enforces the matrix on every call.

editor:filters.title: Editor: finding and editing strings
editor:filters.body:
Placeholders such as {name}, %s, {{name}} or <b> are shown as coloured chips; click one to copy it. A highlighted copy of your translation appears under the text box.

Differences: the Machine diff tab and the Memory (TM) tab can highlight the words that differ from your current translation. Turn Highlight differences off with the checkbox; the choice is remembered in this browser.

What this page is for:
A CAT-style table of every source string next to its translation in one language. You can filter, search, edit inline, open a detail pane for one key, and act on many keys at once.

Which languages you see:
• Admin and the session token see every locale, active and frozen (frozen ones are marked).
• A Translator sees only the locales assigned to them; with none assigned the page says so.
• Supervisors and Developers see their assigned locales, or all when none are assigned.
• Deep links accept locale, namespace, nsPrefix, key and collection.

Toolbar:
• Language – code and English name.
• Workflow chip – the workflow that covers this language; click to open the Workflow page.
• Category – appears when the project has more than one collection; other collections open a file list instead of the table.
• Section – All, dotted key prefixes, or namespaces. With more than 500 source strings All is not selected automatically.
• Status – missing, stale, machine, human, agent, imported, low score (below the threshold, default 0.55), has problems (validation findings), untranslated, verified, pre-translated.
• Search – press Go or Enter. Exact is a case-insensitive substring match done on the server. Regexp and Approximate (edit distance up to 2) run in the browser over up to 5000 rows. Fields to search: key, source, translation, notes.
• Counters – matching, selected and edited this session (reset on reload). Pages hold 250 rows.

Table columns and inline editing:
• Key, source, an editable translation box, a status pill and a score (good from 0.8, middle from 0.6, low below).
• Editing saves when you leave the box if the text changed, or on Ctrl+S / Ctrl+Enter. Esc reverts to the stored text.
• Click a row (not the box or tick) to open the detail pane.

Status meanings:
• missing – no value. stale – the source or its context changed after translation. untranslated – the text equals the source. intentional – equals the source on purpose (Keep as-is). machine – LLM output. human – a person saved it. agent and imported – other channels (ADR-48). Verified is a separate flag, not a status.

What saving does (ADR-48):
• The key must exist in the source and the locale must be a target. Blocking checks (placeholders, plurals, glossary/DNT, HTML and URLs, literals) refuse the save with nothing written; advisory checks warn but allow it.
• The entry is stamped human, written to the catalogue, and recorded in state, scores, history and your activity log. Identical-source keys may receive the same text.

Bulk actions on selected rows:
• Translate selected (cloud runs show a cost estimate first), Re-verify, Clear stale, Purge old machine text (older than 90 days), Requeue broken text, Improve selected, Approve all, Lock/Unlock, Export selection as CSV. Destructive bulk actions show a count and ask to confirm; human, verified and locked keys are always kept.

Permissions:
• Editing needs an approved account with access to the locale. Translate and improve need the Admin or Supervisor role (ADR-39, ADR-58).

operations:general.title: Operations: running commands from the browser
operations:general.body:
What this page is for:
Every CLI command in one place, with a form for its options, live output and permission checks. It runs the same code as the terminal, so results match.

Layout:
• Left list – commands grouped as Analysis, LLM Pipeline, Data, Maintenance and Other; most used first. Commands your role may not run appear locked. Deep links accept ?command= and ?locales=.
• Header – the command name, a badge showing whether an LLM is required, the roles that may run it, a Permissions link and this help.
• Options – locale chips (all ticked by default), a namespace select, the main options for the command, and a collapsed Advanced block holding the rest. Defaults come from the CLI, so llm-localizator <command> --help lists them.

Buttons:
• Run – executes now and streams output when the command supports it.
• Submit to taskqueue – for translate, improve, review, rescore, documents, agent-hardcoded and bakeoff. Long jobs belong in the queue (ADR-28); this needs the tq command on the PATH.
• Dry run – tick it to print what would happen without writing anything.
• Stop – abandons the browser request; the server job may carry on.
• Clear – empties that command's log. Logs are kept when you switch commands.

Cost guard:
• LLM commands first ask for a cost estimate. If the provider is cloud, the batch cost, the cap and the remaining budget are shown and you must confirm (ADR-35).

Special forms:
• Export – format (CSV, XLIFF, JSON or xlsx), layout, which rows to include, optional screenshots; the file downloads.
• Import – pick a CSV, XLIFF, JSON or xlsx file and name who localized it. The page reads only the first file chosen and decides the format from its extension.
• Run workflow – pick a workflow, see which locales it covers, then Dry run or Run. A run that waits for a human is polled every few seconds (ADR-62, ADR-63).
• Scan results – hardcoded-string hits are shown by confidence with Accept, Ignore and Undo. Manual mode only records the choice, request mode opens a review ticket, auto mode adds the key and queues translation (ADR-55).

Who can run what (ADR-39):
• Everyone: validate, status, export, guide. Admin, Supervisor and Developer: estimate-cost, import, agent-backlog. Admin and Developer: scan, discover, doctor, apply. Admin and Supervisor: translate, improve, review, rescore, bakeoff, documents, workflow. Admin only: migrate-state, adopt, init.
• Hidden from this page: web, mcp, add-locale and watch.

progress:general.title: Progress & ETA
progress:general.body:
This page answers: how far along is each language, how fast is it moving, and when will it be done? Use it to plan work and spot locales that are stalled or low quality. It is read-only; it never changes catalogues.

Stages (each stage includes the one before it):
• Localized – the string has a translation that is not stale.
• LLM verified – translated by the model or reused from translation memory.
• Human verified – edited or approved by a person.
• Missing – no current translation (stale strings count as not yet localized).

Summary cards: total source strings and, summed over active locales, how many are localized, LLM verified and human verified. Frozen locales are left out.

Stage table: one stacked bar per locale (human, LLM, localized-only, missing). ASAP locales are highlighted; frozen locales are dimmed.

Progress chart: cumulative localized / LLM / human counts over the last 30 days. Each string is dated by its latest history event, so this is an approximation of past progress, not a full replay.

Throughput by source: keys per day split by who produced them (human, translation memory, machine translation such as DeepL or CTranslate2, AI model, imported). Each key is dated by its latest history event and counted in its current class; keys with no dated event are left out.

Quality chart: rolling 7-day mean LQS score per locale (pick one in the selector). The dashed red line is the 0.55 threshold; dipping under it means recent translations need review. It is built from the current score sidecar, so overwritten scores are not shown.

ETA table: priority (ASAP, normal, frozen), strings remaining, velocity per day and the projected date for 100% localized, 100% LLM verified and 100% human verified. Velocity is the average number of strings written by translate runs over the last 7 days (improve and review rewrite existing strings, so they are not counted), split evenly when a run covers several locales. 'Done' means nothing remains; a dash means velocity is zero or the locale is frozen, so no date can be projected.

Recent runs: latest translate / improve / review runs with locales, model, strings changed and duration.

Use the project selector in the sidebar to switch project; the page reloads with a loading indicator.

usage:general.title: Usage & costs
usage:general.body:
If [privacy] local_only is on, the budget panel says so: cloud providers, remote endpoints and webhooks are blocked and nothing leaves this machine.

This page answers: what did external (cloud) LLM APIs cost, will the monthly cap last, and what would finishing the remaining strings cost? Use it before switching a locale to a paid provider or enabling the dynamic budget mode. It is read-only; it never changes configuration or catalogues, and viewing it spends nothing.

Where the numbers come from:
• Spend, tokens and calls come from the budget ledger (.llm-budget/spend.json). Only cloud providers are metered; local models (Ollama, CTranslate2) cost $0 and are listed separately.
• Strings translated come from run records.
• Cloud is opt-in: [privacy] allow_cloud and [budget] monthly_usd must both be set. While either is off, spend stays $0 and the page shows what cloud would cost instead.

Period: this month, last month, the last 90 days or all time. Export CSV downloads the ledger events of the chosen period (time, locale, provider, model, tokens, USD).

Summary cards:
• Cloud cost – spend in the period, with the change against the previous period of the same length.
• Projected month-end – spend so far divided by elapsed days, times days in the month. Current month only, from day 3, and only when something was spent.
• Tokens – input plus output tokens. Older ledger entries have no token counts; a dash means unknown.
• Avg cost per 1k strings – cloud spend divided by the strings translated for the locales that were billed.

Budget strip: the monthly cap, what is spent and what remains. At 80% it turns amber. At 100% runs fall back to the local provider. Edit the cap and mode in Project config.

Daily chart: spend per day (weekly buckets for long periods).

Recent runs: the latest runs and their cost label; local runs read 0.

usage:providers.title: Usage & costs: Cost by provider
usage:providers.body:
What this panel does:
Splits cloud spend by provider and model, so you can see which paid model accounts for the money.

Columns and bars:
• Provider / model – the cloud service and the model tag that was called.
• Bar and percent – the share of cloud spend in the selected period.
• Calls – how many metered completions were recorded.
• Tokens – input plus output; DeepL shows billed characters instead. A dash means the ledger entry predates token recording.
• USD – amount charged at the configured or published price.

Local row:
Local models are never metered and cost $0. The row shows how many strings they translated in the period, so you can compare it with the cloud rows.

Prices:
An unpriced model is counted at the highest known rate, never at a cheap default, so spend can only be over-counted against the cap. Set [budget.rates] to correct it.

Changing the model for a language is a decision for Settings and needs a fresh bakeoff first (see Model evaluation).

usage:locales.title: Usage & costs: Usage by locale
usage:locales.body:
What this table does:
One row per active target locale: which provider handles it, how much was translated and what it cost in the selected period.

Columns:
• Locale – click to open it in the editor.
• Provider – the backend assigned to the locale. Local backends are tagged local.
• Strings – strings written by translate runs in the period. A run covering several locales is split evenly between them.
• Input / output tokens – cloud calls only. Local models and old ledger entries show a dash.
• Cost – cloud USD for the locale. Local locales are $0.00.
• Per string – cost divided by strings; a dash when either is zero.

Reading it:
• A cloud locale with a high per-string cost may use a model that is larger than the job needs.
• A locale with many strings and no cost runs on your own hardware.

usage:estimate.title: Usage & costs: Estimated cost to complete
usage:estimate.body:
What this table does:
Estimates what it would cost to translate every string that is still due (missing or stale) with each locale's current provider and model. Nothing is sent and nothing is spent.

Columns:
• Remaining – strings due. Frozen locales are listed but left out of the totals.
• Est. tokens – an upper bound from the source text length.
• Est. cost – the ceiling for a cloud locale, from the same price tables a real run is checked against. Local providers show $0.00 (own hardware).
• If cloud – for local locales only: what the same strings would cost on a cloud model. It is a reference for the cloud-versus-local decision and is never added to the totals.

Notes:
• Over budget – the estimate is larger than the budget still available this month. Finish part of it, raise the cap, or use a local model.
• No price – the model has no published price, so no figure is shown rather than a guess.
• Cloud off – the locale uses a cloud provider but allow_cloud is not set, so runs stay local.

On request vs dynamic:
In on_request mode a cloud run only translates keys you name. In dynamic mode it may send every due string whose ceiling fits the remaining budget. Run an exact estimate first in Operations (estimate-cost).

project-config:general.title: Project config
project-config:general.body:
This page edits the project's .llm-localize.toml. Nothing is saved until you press Save all; the whole form is validated first and the file is replaced only if it loads cleanly (an error appears under the tabs and the file is left untouched).

Prompt templates:
• Project description – prepended to every translation prompt.
• Per-language additions – extra instructions for one target language ([prompt.styles.<locale>] notes, max 500 characters).
• Per-model variants – extra guidance used only when that exact model runs; the checkbox translates it into the target language.
• Automatic prompt localization – keep the instruction text in the source language, translate it for every language, or decide per model. The translation is made once per language by the run's own model and cached.
• Advanced – prompt family, per-locale family, glossary path and domains.

Bridge language:
Translate first into an intermediate locale (English or any target), then from it into every other target. Pivot locales override the bridge for single locales. The bridge model, if set, is used only for the bridge locale. Store = No is allowed only when the bridge locale is the source locale.

Glossary sharing:
Attach glossaries owned by other registered projects. They are read-only here. Merge conflicts: project wins (default), shared wins, or project wins and the conflicting terms are listed.

Project identity:
Display name, domain and audience. Domain and audience are added to every translation prompt.

Admins only.

project-config:prompt.title: Project config: Prompt templates
project-config:prompt.body:
What this tab does:
Controls the extra text the engine puts at the top of every translation prompt. Everything here is optional; empty fields add nothing. The text is sent to the local model together with the glossary and the string being translated.

Project description:
• What to write – two to five sentences: what the product is, who uses it, the tone, and rules that apply to every string (for example 'keep UI labels under 30 characters').
• Limit – 2000 characters. It is sent with every request, so shorter text means faster runs on small models.
• Key – [prompt] description.

Per-language prompt additions:
• Add language override – pick one target language and write instructions that apply only to it, such as formal versus informal address or script rules.
• Limit – 500 characters per language. Key – [prompt.styles.<locale>] notes.
• Remove – deletes the note for that language on save.

Per-model prompt variants:
• Why – small models often need blunter instructions than large ones. A variant is added only when that exact model tag runs (for example llama3.2:latest).
• Translate this variant – when ticked, the variant text is translated into the target language before use (see below).
• Limit – 1000 characters per model. Key – [prompt.models."<model>"].

Automatic prompt localization:
• Keep in source language – instructions stay as you wrote them. Safe default.
• Translate for every language – the description, audience, notes and variants are translated once per target language by the model running the job.
• Decide per model – translate only for models whose variant has the box ticked.
• Cached – translations are stored per language and reused until the text changes. If the provider fails the source text is used and the run says so.

Advanced:
• Prompt family – the base template (chat, instruct and so on). A per-locale family overrides it for one language.
• Glossary path and domains – which glossary files the prompt loads.

Saving:
Nothing is written until Save all. Over-long text or an invalid choice shows an error under the tabs and leaves the file untouched.

project-config:bridge.title: Project config: Bridge language
project-config:bridge.body:
What this tab does:
Translates in two hops: first source to a bridge language, then bridge to every other target. Use it when the source language is a poor starting point for some targets, for example translating Polish to Czech through English.

Bridge mode:
• No bridge – every target is translated directly from the source. Default.
• English – the bridge is English.
• Custom – choose any language from the project's targets or the source.

Bridge settings:
• Source language – the project's source locale.
• Bridge locale – must be a target locale or the source. It is translated first, so it is ordered ahead of the languages that depend on it.
• Bridge model – the model used for the bridge language only. Empty means the normal model for that language. Changing models is still an ADR-12 decision: run a bakeoff first.
• Store bridge text – Yes keeps the bridge translations in the catalogue. No discards them after the run and is allowed only when the bridge is the source language.

Pivot locales:
• What they are – a per-language override. A pivot says 'translate this language from that one instead'.
• Precedence – an explicit pivot beats the bridge. Languages without a pivot use the bridge.
• Conflict – a language cannot be both the bridge and have its own pivot; the save is rejected.
• Keys – [bridge] and [locales.pivots].

Tips:
• Start with English as the bridge and compare quality on a small sample before enabling it for all targets.
• Bridge output errors carry into every dependent language, so review the bridge language first.

project-config:glossary.title: Project config: Glossary sharing
project-config:glossary.body:
What this tab does:
Lists the glossaries the prompt uses and lets you attach glossaries owned by other registered projects, so terminology stays consistent across products.

The glossary list:
• Own – this project's glossary file. Edit it on the Glossary page.
• Shared – a glossary from another project. It is read-only here and read-only for this project: only its owner can change it.
• Terms – the number of terms in each file.
• Detach – removes the shared glossary from this project. The other project's file is not touched.

Attach from project:
• Lists registered projects that have a glossary and are not yet attached.
• Attach adds the file to this project's shared list and shows its term count at once.

Merge conflict handling:
• Project wins – when both glossaries translate the same term, yours is used. Default.
• Shared wins – the shared translation replaces yours.
• Project wins and list conflicts – yours is used and the conflicting terms are listed on this tab so you can resolve them. No review flags are created.

Notes:
• Changes apply from the next translate or improve run.
• Key – [prompt] glossary_shared and glossary_conflict. Translation memory sharing is configured separately.

project-config:identity.title: Project config: Project identity
project-config:identity.body:
What this tab does:
Describes the project to the model and to people using the web UI.

Fields:
• Display name – the friendly name shown in headings and the project list. It is not sent to the model. Key – [project] display_name.
• Never translate – read-only list of [exclude] rules (key globs and source regexes) from the toml file.
• Domain – the subject area, for example SaaS or healthcare. Choose a preset or Other for free text. It is added to every prompt and selects domain glossaries. Key – [prompt] domain.
• Audience – who reads the translated text, for example software engineers or patients. Maximum 300 characters. It is added to every prompt as the target audience. Key – [prompt] audience, or [voice] audience when that table exists.
• Tone of voice – how the text should sound, for example friendly and direct. Maximum 300 characters. It is added to every prompt as a Tone line. Key – [voice] tone.

Why it matters:
• Domain and audience change word choice: the same string can need a different register for developers than for the general public.
• Keep them short and concrete; long text slows small models.

Saving:
Empty fields are removed from the file. Use Save all to apply changes from every tab at once.

model-eval:general.title: Model evaluation
model-eval:general.body:
This page answers: which local model should translate each language? It is the evidence step behind ADR-12 (no model swap without a fresh bakeoff Winner). It compares candidate models by translating a fixed set of strings and scoring each result by back-translation (BT): the translation is translated back to the source language and compared with the original. Higher is better, 1.0 is perfect.

What it never does:
It never changes the project configuration. [locales.models], roles and the judge model are edited only in Settings, by a person, after reading the evidence.

Run evaluation tab:
• Model – a single Ollama model tag to test (for example mistral:7b). Leave it empty to queue the full matrix of pinned candidates for the locale.
• Target locale – one of the project's active locales.
• Test set – a sample of the project's own strings, or the built-in corpus.
• Sample size – how many strings to translate (10–500). More strings give steadier scores but take longer.
• Dry run – counts the cells (model × locale) and strings that would be tested. Nothing is translated and nothing is queued.
• Run – queues the job in taskqueue (ADR-28). It never runs in the web server process. If taskqueue is not installed the run is refused.
• Baseline, judge and quality dimensions are shown but disabled: the bakeoff has one fixed scorer (ADR-51), so they cannot be chosen yet.
• Summary cards show the recorded Winner for the chosen locale; the log shows the output of the last dry run or queue request.
• Gold calibration (C.2) – checks the scorer against human-labelled strings. It is a script run from the engine checkout (see docs/model-evaluation.md), not a button.

Results history tab:
Every markdown report in experiments/quality_bakeoff (REPORT.md, LEDGER.md, ANALYSIS.md …) with its date and whether it contains a Winners section. View opens the full text. Reports are written by the bakeoff, never edited here.

Model comparison tab:
The Winners table from REPORT.md – per locale the winning model, its mean BT score (bar), the runner-up and notes. A close runner-up or a note such as 'tie' means the choice is within noise.
• Apply recommendation – appends a dated acknowledgement to apply-notes.md. It does not edit any config: you still change the model in Settings. It stays disabled until the selected report has a Winners section.

Who can use it:
Admins only (running, applying). Recheck at least monthly, or when a new candidate model appears, and always include the incumbent.

tm:concordance.title: Translation memory: Concordance search
tm:concordance.body:
What this tab does:
Finds past translations by text. Translation memory (TM) stores source-to-target pairs so identical or similar strings are reused instead of retranslated. It is separate from the Glossary, which is the termbase of preferred and forbidden terms.

Search fields:
• Query – a word or phrase, for example 'save changes' or '{name}'.
• Locale – the target language to search.
• Source / Target – search the source text, the translation, or both.
• Limit – the maximum number of hits returned.

Result columns:
• Source / Translation – the stored pair. Superseded entries are greyed and italic.
• Key – namespace.key of the first catalogue string with this source text; a dash means no catalogue string matches any more.
• Match – how much of the source string the query covers. 100% is shown in bold.
• Score – the stored LQS quality score; green is 0.80 or higher, amber is lower.
• Status – human, machine, imported, agent, or stale (superseded by a newer entry; it cannot be reused).

Actions:
• Use → – opens the editor on that key with the translation ready to insert.
• Nothing here changes the TM; searching is read-only.

tm:leverage.title: Translation memory: Leverage report
tm:leverage.body:
What this tab does:
Shows where the current translations came from, so you can see how much work translation memory saves. It is read-only.

Summary cards:
• TM reuse – strings filled from memory without calling a model.
• LLM generated – strings translated by a model.
• Human edited – strings written or approved by a person.
• Agent / imported – strings from agent edits or TMX import.

Per-locale table:
• One bar per locale, split by origin, as a share of classified string-locale pairs.
• Frozen locales are marked and left out of automatic runs.
• Coverage, stale and missing counts show how much is still open.

How to read it:
• Higher TM reuse means cheaper, faster and more consistent output.
• Low reuse in a mature locale suggests the TM is empty or was not imported; use Import TMX to seed it.
• Strings that are stale were translated from an older source text and no longer count as current.

tm:browse.title: Translation memory: Browse
tm:browse.body:
What this tab does:
Lists the raw entries stored for one locale so you can audit what memory will reuse.

Filters:
• Locale – the target language. Changing it reloads the list.
• Provider – all providers, or only entries written by one model, human, import or agent.
• Text filter – press Enter to match source or translation text.
• Up to 250 rows are shown; the count is displayed in the toolbar.

Columns:
• Namespace / Key – the catalogue string whose source text matches the entry, when one exists. Entries whose text left the catalogue show a dash.
• Source / Translation – the stored pair.
• Provider / Model – who produced it.
• Score – the LQS quality score, green at 0.80 or higher.
• Status – human, machine, imported, agent, or stale.
• Click a column header to sort; the header stays visible while you scroll.

Export:
• Export TMX – downloads the displayed locale as <locale>.tmx. See the Import and export help for the file format.

tm:import-export.title: Translation memory: Import and export
tm:import-export.body:
Export TMX:
• Choose a locale and press Export. The file <locale>.tmx is downloaded; nothing is written to the project.
• TMX is the standard exchange format, so the file works in other translation tools.

Import TMX:
• File – the TMX file to read. Only units that contain the project's source language and the chosen locale are used.
• Locale – the target language the units are imported into.
• Conflict rule – skip existing keeps what is already stored; overwrite if higher replaces an entry only when the imported score is better; always overwrite replaces every match.
• Dry run – previews the counts (added, overwritten, skipped) and writes nothing. Untick it to apply.

After an import:
• Imported entries get the 'imported' provider.
• Catalogue strings whose source text matches get a history event so the change is traceable.
• Units with no matching catalogue string are still stored and will be reused when that text appears.

Who can use it:
Importing needs edit permission; exporting is read-only.

dashboard:general.title: Dashboard: project overview
dashboard:general.body:
What this page is for:
The first screen after sign-in: how complete and how good the translations are, what needs a decision, and the next step to take.

Header:
• Project name and a line with the number of source strings, target locales and the time of the last run.
• + Add locale opens Settings at the locales tab (Admin only), Open editor and Ops are shortcuts.

Tiles:
• Total strings – source keys and namespaces.
• Avg coverage – the plain mean of every locale's coverage, frozen locales included.
• Pending review – open review tickets across all targets; the link opens the queue and the sidebar badge shows the same number.
• Avg quality – the mean stored quality score of the first active target, based on back-translation.

Cloud budget card:
• Spend this month against the [budget] monthly ceiling, a bar that turns red from 90 percent, what is left, the budget mode and a projection once the month is three days old. A small chart shows the last six months.
• Local models cost nothing and are not counted. A local-only project (privacy local_only) shows a note instead of a number; with no ceiling and cloud off it says cloud translation is off.

Coverage by locale:
• One row per language with translated / total, a percentage bar (green from 80 percent, red under 50, grey when frozen), an Edit link and a play button that translates just that locale.
• Translated means a catalogue value whose source hash still matches. Missing means no value or no state. Stale means the source or its context changed. Skipped keys are not counted.
• The workflow line shows the workflow covering the locale and its last run.

Quick actions:
• Run translation for all active locales, review pending strings, export a CSV handoff including frozen locales, validate all locales.
• Translating needs the Admin or Supervisor role and respects the cloud cost gate.

Other cards:
• Recent activity – the last eight runs with counts and locales.
• Quality distribution – six score bands from under 0.5 to 0.9 and above; excellent from 0.8, fair 0.6 to 0.8, low under 0.6.
• Quality trend – coverage and weekly edit-rate over 90 days.
• Coverage by screen – the top screens named in context notes, with pending counts.
• Hardcoded strings – decisions from the last scan, shown only when a scan is cached.
• English flagged for review – source strings someone flagged; hidden when empty and from Translators.

Getting started:
• A checklist (environment, project, languages, model, optional apply mode, translate, review, optional ship) shows how many steps are done and a button for the next one. It disappears when nothing is left.

analysis:general.title: Pre-translation analysis
analysis:general.body:
A read-only pre-flight check. It tells you what a translate run would touch before you press the button. Nothing is written and nothing is queued until you choose Queue translate jobs.

What you see:
• Total source strings – every source string in scope, with its word count.
• 100% TM matches – due strings whose exact source already sits in translation memory; translate reuses them without a model call.
• Fuzzy matches – due strings with a similar TM entry (55% or more overlap). They still go to the model, with the match as context.
• New / no match – due strings with nothing similar in TM.
• Est. cloud cost – a ceiling for paying cloud providers; local providers cost nothing.

Scope:
• Due means missing, empty or stale in the target locale – the same set translate and estimate-cost use.
• Frozen locales are shown dimmed and left out of every total and out of the queue action.
• The namespace filter narrows everything to one namespace.

Header actions:
• Re-analyze – reads the catalogues, state and TM again.
• Export report – downloads the per-locale table as CSV.

analysis:breakdown.title: Analysis: Leverage by locale
analysis:breakdown.body:
Each row buckets the due strings of one locale by the best translation-memory match.

Bands:
• 100% – exact source match; reused as is.
• Fuzzy 75–99 – close match; the model starts from it, review is cheap.
• Fuzzy 55–74 – weak match (55% is the lowest overlap searched); treat as new.
• No match – full model translation.

The bar shows the four bands in that order, green to grey.

Estimates:
• Est. effort – strings that are not exact matches, times the measured seconds per string from your past single-locale translate runs. It shows a dash until a locale has at least 20 measured strings.
• Est. cloud cost – a ceiling, not a bill. Local providers show $0.00. A missing price shows not recorded.
• Active locales total – frozen locales are excluded.

analysis:repetitions.title: Analysis: Internal repetitions
analysis:repetitions.body:
A repetition is a source string used by more than one key. The list shows the most repeated ones, the first key that uses them, and how many namespaces they appear in.

What it means for a run:
• Translate does not copy identical sources between keys; each key is translated on its own (ADR-43).
• Saving one of them in the editor copies the text to its empty twins that pass the same checks.
• Exact TM hits are still reused, so a repeated string is cheap once one copy is in memory.

What to do: if a repeated string is wrong everywhere, fix it once in the editor.

analysis:providers.title: Analysis: Provider assignment
analysis:providers.body:
Shows which provider and model will translate each active locale, grouped when they share both.

Things to know:
• Assignments come from Settings → Translation engine; change them there.
• A cloud locale is billed. The page shows the ceiling and the remaining monthly budget, and warns when the ceiling is higher.
• If a cloud provider is configured but cloud is off (allow_cloud, or no monthly budget), the locale runs locally and the page says so.
• Do not swap a model just because of this page: change models only after a bakeoff win (ADR-12).

analysis:queue.title: Analysis: Queueing translate
analysis:queue.body:
Queue translate jobs submits one translate job to the taskqueue for the active, non-frozen locales (and the selected namespace, if any). It asks for confirmation first.

Notes:
• Needs the translate permission; otherwise the server refuses and the message appears under the button.
• It is disabled when nothing is due, or when the cloud ceiling is above the remaining budget.
• Go to Operations opens the translate form with these locales filled in, so you can do a dry run or change options first.

workflow:general.title: Workflow automation
workflow:general.body:
A workflow is a small script built from blocks. It starts at "When workflow runs" and the blocks below it run top to bottom, in the order you stack them. Workflows are saved in the project config under [workflows.<name>].

The strings the script works on flow through it as one group. Blocks like If split the group; blocks like Auto-approve or Human review ticket take strings out of it.

• Drag a block from the palette into the script, or click it to add it at the highlighted spot (click a thin line between blocks to choose the spot).
• Use ▲ ▼ ✕ on a block to move or delete it. Undo and redo are in the header.
• Save writes every workflow to the config.
• + New workflow offers templates: the default pipeline, re-route existing scores, auto-approve only, or blank.

Nothing is committed to git. Already verified strings are never processed again.

workflow:blocks.title: Workflow: Blocks
workflow:blocks.body:
Run (yellow) – LLM work on the strings that reach the block:
• Translate – missing and stale strings.
• Re-score – back-translation and quality score. Put it before a score condition so the condition reads fresh values.
• Improve – re-translates low scorers. Skipped during the improve cooldown; after the block's max loops (0 to 5, set on the block itself; default from the workflow, 2) failed passes the string gets a review ticket instead.
• LLM review – the review pass.
• Validate – runs the catalogue checks (placeholders, ICU, length...) on the strings that reach it. Findings are logged, nothing is changed and the strings keep flowing; follow it with Flag or a condition to act.

Starting points: the New workflow dialog offers presets from the server, including TM → LLM → validate → route (Translate uses the translation memory before the model).

Control (orange):
• If … Then … Else – splits strings by a condition: quality score ≥ or ≤ a number from 0 to 1, or status / locale / namespace is / is not a value. If blocks nest.
• Stop – ends the script for the strings that reach it.

Result (green) – strings leave the flow:
• Auto-approve – marks them verified (verified_by=workflow); the provider is unchanged.
• Human review ticket – opens a review ticket (reason low_score).

Mark (blue): Flag for admin adds strings to the flag list and they keep flowing.
Notify (purple): Send webhook posts a short summary to the project webhook when the run ends, whatever the Notification setting says. The webhook URL is project-wide ([notify] webhook) and appears in Workflow settings when the script has this block.

Strings that reach the end of the script without a Result block simply end – there is no implicit ticket. The count on a block is how many strings reached it in the last run.

Limits: 100 blocks, nested 6 deep. Soft warnings (a score check before any Re-score, an empty branch, blocks after Stop) never block saving.

workflow:run.title: Workflow: Running
workflow:run.body:
• Dry run – walks the script and shows how many strings each block would handle. Nothing is changed, queued or recorded.
• Re-route only – skips the Translate and Re-score blocks and works on the scores that already exist.
• Run – executes the whole script.

With a task queue (tq) on the PATH, LLM blocks (Translate, Re-score, Improve, LLM review) are queued and the run shows Waiting. The page checks the queue every few seconds and continues the script when the task has finished, so the blocks after it see the new results. You can leave the page and come back. A failed task marks the run failed; Cancel run stops a waiting run.

Without a task queue the LLM blocks run inside the request and the page waits until the run is done.

Save changes before a run.

workflow:config.title: Workflow: Settings
workflow:config.body:
Settings of the selected workflow.

• Workflow name – the workflow name. Renaming changes the key in the config.
• Locales – limits this workflow to the chosen locales. All active locales means every target that no other workflow claims. A locale in several scopes uses the first workflow alphabetically (a warning is shown); a locale in no scope uses the workflow named default.
• Applies to – the locales this workflow handles right now, including unsaved edits.
• Notification – None, or Webhook: after a run that created review tickets or flags, a short summary is posted. The Webhook URL field (shown for Webhook or when the script has a Send webhook block) is project-wide: it is saved to [notify] webhook and shared by all workflows. Leave it empty to keep the stored URL. Email is not available.

Webhook bodies are {event, project, ts, data}; set [notify] format = slack in the config for a Slack-style {text} body.
• Max loops for Improve is set on the Improve block itself.

Duplicate copies the workflow (locales cleared, unsaved until Save). Copy to project… adds it to another project, dropping locales that project does not have; it refuses to replace an existing name unless you tick Overwrite.

Tickets are assigned to the owner from the [ownership] table when one matches.

workflow:history.title: Workflow: Last run
workflow:history.body:
Totals from the last real run of this workflow. Dry runs are not recorded.

• Last run – when the run finished.
• Auto-approved, Improved, Human review, Flagged, LLM reviewed – how many strings each Result/Run/Mark block handled, with the share of strings that were routed (percentages can add up to less than 100% when strings were skipped by the improve cooldown or ended without a Result block).

The numbers on the blocks in the canvas are the per-block counts of the same run ('all' means the whole scope).

glossary:general.title: Glossary
glossary:general.body:
This page answers: which terms must be translated a specific way, kept untranslated, or avoided? Every term here is injected into the translation prompt for its locale, so this is the strongest lever on consistent terminology (brand names, product vocabulary, legal terms).

Header and toolbar:
• Subtitle – the number of terms, including do-not-translate rows. It ignores the search box.
• Search terms – matches the term name plus all locale text, forbidden words and notes. Do-not-translate rows match on the term name only.
• Locales – choose which locale columns are shown (the last visible one cannot be hidden). The choice is remembered in this browser per project; the default is the active, non-frozen targets.
• + Add term – opens the term dialog.

Table:
• Term / Domain / Type – the source term, the glossary file (domain) it lives in, and its type.
• preferred – the term has an approved translation per locale. The cell shows the preferred text or a dash when none is set; forbidden words appear as tags with the note below.
• do not translate – the term stays in the source language in every locale (brand names, code identifiers).
• Edit / ✕ – edit a row or delete it. Delete is immediate and has no confirmation.

How terms reach the model (ADR-29):
• Only terms that actually occur in the batch being translated are put in the prompt, so a large glossary does not slow runs.
• Validation uses the same data: V04 (a forbidden word appears) is blocking, V13 (an approved term is missing) is advisory. Both apply only when the source contains the term.

Where it is stored:
• In the project's glossary file or folder, as JSON: {"doNotTranslate": [...], "terms": {term: {locale: text, locale_forbidden: [...], locale_note: ...}}}. A folder holds one <domain>.json per domain; a single file only supports the global domain.
• Saves happen under the project mutation lock and the glossary is reloaded at once.
• Shared glossaries attached in Project config are read-only and do not appear here (ADR-42).

Who can use it:
• Any approved signed-in user can add, edit and delete terms, including Translators and Developers (ADR-58 left this open on purpose). Locale scoping does not apply to glossary edits.

Caveats:
• Only the global domain is always applied. Other domain files affect prompts only when mapped by namespace or context domain.
• Changes take effect from the next translate or improve run; existing translations are not rewritten.

glossary:modal.title: Glossary: Add or edit a term
glossary:modal.body:
What this dialog does:
Creates or changes one glossary entry. Nothing is saved until you press Add term or Save.

Fields:
• Term – the source-language term, for example 'namespace'. Required, one line, at most 200 characters. It is locked when editing.
• Type – preferred (translate this way) or do not translate (keep as is). Locked when editing.
• Domain – the glossary file the term is stored in. Default global. Letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', up to 64 characters. With a single-file glossary only global is allowed; with a folder, <domain>.json is created on demand. Locked when editing.
• Translations table – one row per locale: Preferred (the approved translation), Forbidden (semicolon-separated words that must not appear) and Notes (guidance for the model and reviewers). Show all locales / Show enabled locales only toggles the list.

Rules:
• Add is refused when the term already exists in any domain or is already do-not-translate.
• Leaving Preferred empty removes that locale; leaving Forbidden empty removes the forbidden list.
• For a do-not-translate term the locale fields are ignored and disabled.
• Other keys on the entry, such as inflected forms, are preserved on save.
• Server errors (duplicate, invalid domain) are shown inside the dialog.

glossary:csv.title: Glossary: CSV import and export
glossary:csv.body:
Export CSV:
• Downloads glossary.csv with the columns term, locale, translation, forbidden, note (plus forms when some term has inflected forms).
• A row with an empty locale marks a do-not-translate term.
• All domains are merged into one file; the domain is not included.

Import CSV:
• Choose a file. The first step is always a dry run: nothing is written and a summary such as 'applied=12 skipped=3 (dry-run)' is shown with an Apply import button.
• Apply import writes the terms. The same file with dry run off is posted again.
• The browser import uses the skip rule: any term that already exists, in any domain, is left untouched and never updated. Overwrite and TBX are available only on the command line (llm-localizator glossary import --conflict overwrite).
• A malformed row aborts the whole import and the error names the row number; the header must match the export columns.
• New terms land in the global domain, because export does not carry the domain.

Who can use it:
• Export is open to every role. Import is allowed for Admin, Supervisor and Developer, not for Translators.

review:general.title: Review queue
review:general.body:
This page answers: which strings need a human decision, who owns them, and what has been said about them? It is the worklist behind quality tiers, workflow rules, visual findings and source-review flags.

Left pane:
• Locale – tickets are kept per target locale. The first target is selected by default.
• Search key or reason – filters the loaded list by namespace, key and reason.
• + New ticket – opens a ticket by hand.
• Filter tabs – Open, In review (in progress), Closed (done) and Blocked. The status filter is applied on the server.
• Filter tabs carry live counts. Each card shows the type badge, #RQ-nnn id, age, key · locale, a title or excerpt, assignee and comment count; newest first.
• The sidebar badge counts all open, in-progress and blocked tickets across target locales and refreshes on every page.

Where tickets come from:
• translate – a medium or high-risk string with incomplete context is blocked and gets a ticket with reason needs_context:<reasons> (ADR-26).
• Quality tiers – [quality.tiers] with reasons tier:human or tier:review (ADR-52).
• Workflow rules – the final 'Human review ticket' result block, reason low_score (ADR-62).
• Visual findings – ingest-visual (ADR-27).
• Source review – flag-source, reason source-review (ADR-53).
• Scan decisions – accepting a hit while [apply] mode = request gives reason localize-request:<id> (ADR-55).

Ownership and escalation:
• A new ticket without an explicit assignee takes its owner from the [ownership] table (first matching glob wins).
• [review] escalate_after_days (default 0 = off) makes sync post the [notify] webhook once per overdue ticket.

Storage:
• Tickets live in .llm-review/<locale>.jsonl (ADR-26): id, namespace, key, reason, status, assignee, comments, timestamps. New tickets are appended; comment and status changes rewrite that locale's file atomically.

Who can use it:
• Any approved user for the locales in their scope; a Translator can work the whole page for assigned locales. The comment author is always the signed-in username.

review:ticket.title: Review queue: Ticket detail
review:ticket.body:
What this panel shows:
• Header – type badge, #RQ-nnn id, title, who opened it and when, with an assign dropdown, a status dropdown (applied immediately) and Close ticket (sets done).
• String context – source and current translation side by side, the LQS score bar, the scorer and signals.
• Open in editor – jumps to the editor on this locale and key so you can fix the text.

Working a ticket:
• Status and assignee – change them from the header dropdowns; each change is recorded as an event in the discussion with who did it and when.
• Discussion – the opening event, status and assignee events and comments, in time order.
• Post – adds your comment. Post and resolve – adds it and sets the status to done.
• Also improve via LLM – after resolving, runs improve for this key. Only Admin and Supervisor may run improve; for other roles the option is denied.
• Related – other tickets for the same namespace and key or with the same reason; click one to open it.

Special tickets:
• localize-request:<id> – closing it (Post and resolve or a done status) applies the scan request (ADR-55). If the scan decision is still accepted, the source key is written and a translate task is queued. Applying twice is harmless.

Caveats:
• The Open tab shows only open tickets; in-progress and blocked ones sit under their own tabs.

review:new.title: Review queue: New ticket
review:new.body:
What this dialog does:
Opens a review ticket for one string by hand, for example when you notice a bad translation or need context from a developer.

Fields:
• Key and Locale – which string (the namespace is the part before the first dot). Both required.
• Type – why it needs review (reason). Default needs_context.
• Title – optional one-line summary shown on the card.
• Description – becomes the first comment. It requires an author.
• Assignee – optional. Without one, the owner comes from the [ownership] table.
• Author – who you are; remembered between tickets. The server uses the signed-in username regardless.

Behaviour:
• If an open ticket already exists for that key it is refreshed instead of duplicated: the reason is updated, and so is the assignee when given.
• Cancel closes the dialog without saving; Create writes to .llm-review/<locale>.jsonl.

users:general.title: Users & roles
users:general.body:
This page answers: who can sign in, who is waiting for approval, and what can each person edit? It is for Admins only; other roles see 'Admin required' and the link is hidden.

Accounts:
• Accounts are shared by the whole server, not per project. They are stored in the default project's state directory (users.json, sessions.json). The project switcher only changes catalogues.
• The first person to register becomes an approved Admin. Later registrations are pending with no role until approved.
• Registration needs a username of at least 2 characters and a password of at least 8. Passwords are hashed with scrypt. Sessions last 14 days.
• There is no email, OAuth or password reset (ADR-39).

Invite:
• + Invite user shows the registration link <origin>/register. No email is sent; copy the link and share it. New accounts then appear under Pending approval.

Pending approval:
• Each row has a role selector (default Translator), language chips (× to remove, + add to add) and Approve / Deny. Admin approval ignores chips and grants all languages.
• Deny clears the role; the person disappears from both lists but stays in users.json. The page has no way to re-approve them.

Active users:
• Filter users – client-side by username.
• Columns: User (with a short id and '(you)'), Role, Language access, Last active (currently always a dash) and Remove.
• Changing a role or a language chip saves immediately and takes effect at once, without confirmation.
• Remove deletes the user and their sessions. It refuses to remove yourself or the last Admin.

Caveats:
• Language chips only restrict non-Admin roles. A Translator with no chips can access no locales.
• Approving a role change does not stop you demoting the last Admin; do not do that.
• Translators and Developers stay on the default project; Admin and Supervisor can switch.

users:roles.title: Users & roles: Role guide
users:roles.body:
The four cards summarise the default permission matrix (ops/permissions.py, ADR-39). Settings → Permissions can adjust individual operations.

• Admin – full access to all languages; invites and manages users; runs the LLM pipeline; configures projects and models.
• Supervisor – edits and approves assigned languages; runs validate, rescore and improve; sees quality scores and history; cannot manage users.
• Translator – edits assigned languages only; sees source strings and context; cannot run LLM operations and cannot see other locales. An override can never grant a Translator the translate operation.
• Developer – runs scan, discover, doctor and push-strings; validate, export and release-diff; cannot translate or improve; cannot manage users.

How the matrix is used:
• Operations: translate, improve, review and rescore are Admin and Supervisor; scan, discover, doctor and push-strings are Admin and Developer; export, validate and status are open to everyone; import is Admin, Supervisor and Developer; suggest is Admin, Supervisor and Translator.
• Locale scope: Admin and the startup token see all locales. Translators see only the locales assigned as chips. Supervisor and Developer are restricted only when they have chips.
• A request with the valid startup token and no session runs as Admin; a signed-in user always wins over the token.

activity:general.title: Team activity
activity:general.body:
This page answers: who changed which translations, how, and when? It is a read-only audit of attributed edits for Admins and Supervisors; other roles see 'Admin or Supervisor required'.

Filters:
• Translator – 'All translators' or one person. Choosing one re-queries the server for that user and also narrows the table to them; reset it to see everyone.
• Trigger – all triggers or one kind of action. It filters the timeline only, not the translators table.

Translators table:
• Columns: Translator, Changes (total), By trigger (for example 'web-edit 5 · web-verify 2') and Last activity.
• Click a row to filter by that person.

Timeline:
• Newest first, capped at 200 events. Each row has the relative time, username, trigger, locale and namespace/key.

Triggers:
• web-edit, web-revert, web-verify, web-unverify – actions in the web editor.
• workflow-verify – a workflow Auto-approve block.
• Variants ending in -full are companion rows for full-key changes.

Where the data comes from (ADR-46):
• The ledger file is <state>/translator_activity.jsonl. A row is written only when a signed-in user performs the action; the identity comes from the session, never the request body.
• The file keeps the last 50,000 lines. It survives history compaction (20 events per key).

Caveats:
• Edits made through the CLI, agents or the shared startup token are unattributed and do not appear here.

setup:project.title: Guided setup: Your project
setup:project.body:
What this wizard does:
Takes a project from zero to a first translation without editing .llm-localize.toml by hand. It has five steps: Your project, Languages, Model, About your product, Finish. Back and Next move between steps; nothing is saved until the last step.

Step 1: Your project
• The summary line shows what was found: source keys, namespaces, format and source language. 'Checking your message files…' appears while it loads.
• Language your strings are written in – the source locale. Changing it removes that locale from the targets and only tells the tool how to read your files.
• Where are my message files? – open it when detection is wrong. Format is one of json-nested, json-flat, yaml, po, arb or android-xml. Path template says where files live, for example messages/{locale}/{namespace}.json.

It is the same engine as the 'guide' command and the dashboard Getting started card (ADR-50). The wizard always uses the server's default project; there is no project selector.

setup:languages.title: Guided setup: Languages
setup:languages.body:
What this step does:
Chooses the languages to translate into. You can add more later in Settings → Locales.

• Chips at the top show your current choice ('Nothing selected yet.' when empty).
• Search languages filters a checkbox list of known language profiles with name, code and a right-to-left tag. The source language is not listed.
• Not listed? Any language code works – type a code such as sw or pt-AO and press Add. The accepted pattern is a 2–3 letter code optionally followed by region or script parts. Errors: the text does not look like a language code, or it is your source language.

Caveat:
• Save replaces the targets with what you picked here; it does not add to them. If targets already exist, do not save with nothing selected, as that empties the list.

setup:model.title: Guided setup: Model
setup:model.body:
What this step does:
Chooses the model that translates. It writes only the 'default' entry of [locales.models]; per-locale models you set earlier are left alone. Changing the model of a working project is an ADR-12 decision that needs a fresh bakeoff.

Ollama:
• Your text stays on this machine. Pick an installed model from the list, or type a tag such as llama3.2 when none is listed.
• 'Ollama is not reachable' – start it with 'ollama serve' and reload. 'No models are installed yet' – run 'ollama pull llama3.2'.

Other providers:
• The provider kind is shown; type the model name that provider expects.

Test it:
• Sends one short string to the model to prove it answers, using the first active target locale. It times out after 120 seconds.
• For any provider other than Ollama you are asked first, because it is a real paid call; the server also refuses without confirmation (ADR-35).
• A successful test is remembered in the guide state. The test is optional and does not block Next.

setup:product.title: Guided setup: About your product
setup:product.body:
What this step does:
Writes one sentence about your product into [prompt] domain. It goes into every translation prompt and is the biggest single lever on terminology and tone.

How to write it:
• Say what it is and who uses it, for example 'a hotel booking app for business travellers'.
• Keep it short. Long text slows small models.
• Leave it blank to keep the default 'a software application'.

You can refine domain, audience and style later in Project config.

setup:finish.title: Guided setup: Finish
setup:finish.body:
What this step does:
Shows a summary and saves it. The summary lists source language, languages you translate into, model and product description.

Save:
• Writes .llm-localize.toml under the mutation lock: [project] source_locale, [locales] targets, [locales.models] default, [prompt] domain and [catalog] format and path.
• The new file is loaded as a probe first; if it does not parse, the old file is kept. On success the server state is rebuilt.
• With no languages selected a warning appears: there is nothing to translate yet.

After saving:
• The guide shows the next step, or 'Everything is set up'.
• Run first translation – translates the chosen languages right now, in this server process (not through the task queue), so it can take a long time. Only Admin may run it. For big projects use Operations or the CLI with taskqueue instead (ADR-28).
• Open the editor and Go to the dashboard are shortcuts.

Who can use it:
• Admins only (the startup token counts as Admin).

settings:providers.title: Settings: LLM providers
settings:providers.body:
What this card does:
Lists the LLM endpoints the engine can call. A provider is a connection (Ollama, CTranslate2 or a paid cloud service); which model on it translates which language is chosen in the next card.

Table and actions:
• Name, Type, Endpoint, Models and Status – the provider's label, its kind (shown as a badge), where it is reached, the models it offers, and a status dot from the last check.
• + Add provider – opens a dialog for a new named provider (ADR-47).
• Edit – changes the endpoint, kind or name.
• ✕ – removes a provider after confirmation. The provider named 'default' cannot be removed.

Local versus cloud:
• Local providers (Ollama, CT2) keep text on this machine and cost nothing.
• Cloud providers are metered and need [privacy] allow_cloud and a monthly budget (ADR-35). Watch the spend on the Usage page.

Caveats:
• Removing a provider that locales still use leaves those assignments pointing at nothing; reassign them first.
• Changing which model a language uses is an ADR-12 decision and needs a fresh bakeoff.

settings:engine.title: Settings: Engine
settings:engine.body:
What this card does:
Picks the engine: one setting that chooses the provider and model for every step of the pipeline (translate, back-translation scoring, improve). Built-in engines cover Claude Haiku, DeepSeek, OpenAI and local Ollama models sized for 4, 8 or 16 GB of GPU memory.

Table and actions:
• Roles – the provider and model each step uses right now, including locales that keep their own model.
• Evidence – benchmarked (won a bakeoff), approved waiver, smoke test only, or not benchmarked.
• This machine – whether the API key is set and the GPU is large enough.
• Use this engine – writes [engine] id to .llm-localize.toml. Keys that would hide the engine are removed; per-locale models stay.

Cloud and budget:
Cloud engines send text to a paid API. Turning cloud on ([privacy] allow_cloud) and the monthly cap ([budget] monthly_usd) stay in your config file; this card never writes them.

settings:quality.title: Settings: Quality scoring
settings:quality.body:
What this card does:
Sets the quality-score threshold.

• Score threshold (flag below) – a number from 0 to 1, default 0.55. A string whose LQS score is lower is flagged as low score. LQS is a back-translation based score: the translation is translated back and compared with the source (ADR-20, ADR-51).
• Reset threshold – returns the field to the default.
• Save changes – writes the value to the configuration.

Where it is used:
• Validation and review flag low scorers, the Progress page draws the same line on its quality chart, and workflow score conditions compare against absolute values you set on the block.
• Lowering the threshold hides weak translations; raising it creates more review work. Change it deliberately, using the distribution on the Progress page.

operations:validate.title: Operations: validate
operations:validate.body:
What it does:
Runs every catalogue check (placeholders, plurals, ICU syntax, glossary and do-not-translate terms, inline do-not-translate elements (V42: translate="no" or class="notranslate" must survive verbatim), HTML and URLs, whitespace, scripts, length and more) on the translated files. No model is called and nothing is written unless you tick Write flags.

Options:
• Locales and Namespace – limit the run. Empty means every target locale.
• Check layout (V28) – compares translations against the context screenshots when a note names a screen or image.
• Check numbers (V38) – locale-aware number and date-order checks. Off by default.
• Check expansion (V14) – the noisy expansion-band advisory.
• Semantic advisory checks – the whitespace, punctuation and coherence family (V17, V21 to V31). Refused on an unscoped catalogue above 500 source keys; pick a namespace instead.
• Unused keys (V41) – also runs the source scanner and lists keys no code references. Needs [scan]; keys matching unused_allow are skipped.
• Strict – warnings count as errors.
• Format – text, github (workflow annotations) or json.
• Diff scope – only namespaces touched by listed files.
• Quiet – print only the summary line.
• Write flags for improve – appends selected findings to the flags file so the improve pass picks them up.

Result and exit status:
• Findings are listed per locale and key with a code such as V02; the code links to the rule in docs/checks. Exit 0 is clean, 2 warnings only, 1 errors (1 for warnings too with Strict).

Who may run it: every role.

operations:status.title: Operations: status
operations:status.body:
What it does:
Shows per-locale coverage from the state files. For each language it lists the percentage translated, how many keys are done, stale or missing, and a leverage line. No model is used.

Options:
• Missing – list every missing or stale key with its reason instead of the summary counts. Useful as a translator's work list or a CI check.
• By screen – groups coverage by the screen named in each key's context note, least complete first.
• Collection – default messages. A file collection lists each file with its coverage; a remote collection (a database behind the content API) calls that API and reports each unit's source language and what is missing, stale, machine or human. Remote status needs the network; file status does not.
• Format – text or json.

Reading the numbers:
• Translated means a catalogue value whose source hash still matches. Stale means the English text or its context changed afterwards. Missing means no value or no state entry. Frozen languages are included.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:scan.title: Operations: scan
operations:scan.body:
What it does:
Reads your application source for t() call sites and for hardcoded user-visible strings. It records which message keys are used where (usage artefacts) and counts strings that were never put into a catalogue. It never calls a model.

Options:
• Adapter – overrides the scanner configured in [scan]. The adapter knows how your framework calls its translation function.
• Out dir – where the usage artefacts go.
• Report only – writes nothing, including the usage files.
• Format – text, github or json.
• Strict – exit 1 if any hardcoded string is found, which makes it usable as a CI gate.

Related commands:
• Agent-hardcoded produces the paste-ready report for an agent to fix the source; scan itself is the quick count.
• Scan-decide, patch and apply turn findings into catalogue keys.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:discover.title: Operations: discover
operations:discover.body:
What it does:
Looks for directories named after locales (for example a sibling folder per language) and proposes them as text collections. It writes nothing; copy a proposal you agree with into .llm-localize.toml, or accept it with scan-decide using the collection kind.

Options:
• Format – text or json.

When to use it:
• Right after adding a project that keeps documents, legal pages or help content outside the message catalogue. The proposals appear as extra categories in the editor once configured.
• A directory is only proposed when its layout looks like one folder per language, so an unusual structure may need a manual entry. See docs/configuration.md.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:places.title: Operations: places
operations:places.body:
What it does:
Shows and sets the translation policy for each text place (a namespace, or NS:KEYGLOB inside one). Policies: auto (translated by sweeps), request (only when explicitly asked), review (translated, then held for human approval), never (skipped by sweeps and validation).

Actions:
• list – every namespace with its key count and effective policy.
• set PLACE --policy P – writes [places.PLACE] policy into the project toml in place, keeping comments.
• unset PLACE – removes the explicit entry so the default applies again.

Notes:
• The most specific pattern wins, then the [places] default (auto, so existing projects behave as before). Today never is enforced everywhere keys are skipped; request and review are recorded and shown but not yet enforced by sweeps (ADR-104).

operations:projects.title: Operations: projects
operations:projects.body:
What it does:
Manages the machine-level list of registered projects (the name-to-folder index in your home directory). It never edits a project's own config, catalogues or state.

Actions:
• list – shows every registered project and flags those whose config file is missing.
• remove NAME – unregisters one project; its files stay exactly where they are.
• rename OLD NEW – changes the registry name; refused when NEW is already taken.
• prune – unregisters every project whose config file no longer exists.

Typical use:
• After moving or deleting a checkout, run prune, then re-add the project with init from its new folder. Re-running init --force on an existing project now merges into its config instead of overwriting comments and other sections.

CLI only for now: this edits a per-user file, not a project, so it has no web endpoint.

operations:verify.title: Operations: verify
operations:verify.body:
What it does:
Runs a read-only health check of a whole project on a throwaway copy, so your checkout is never touched. It fingerprints the project, runs init and re-init, checks that catalogues load and save back unchanged, runs status and validate, scans for hardcoded strings cold and warm, and finally confirms the engine changed no source file (ADR-32).
