No model is called.

Options:
• Path – the project directory to check (required).
• Profile – quick (default), standard or deep. Later profiles add more stages.
• Only and Skip – run or leave out named stages such as S4.
• Resume – continue an earlier run by id; finished stages are not repeated.
• Out – where run records and VERIFY.md are written.

Reading the result:
• Each stage reports pass, degraded, fail, unsupported or skipped. Exit 0 means all pass, 1 any fail, 2 only degraded or unsupported.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:estimate-cost.title: Operations: estimate-cost
operations:estimate-cost.body:
What it does:
Calculates the maximum amount in US dollars to translate the due strings (missing, empty and stale) with a cloud provider. No API call is made, so it is free and safe to run at any time.

How to read the answer:
• max_usd assumes one request per string. batch_usd assumes the configured batch size, which is closer to a real run. Actual usage after a run is what you are billed.
• Local providers (Ollama, CT2) report zero cost.

Options:
• Locales and Namespace – restrict what is counted.
• Keys – list namespace.key entries. Under the on_request budget mode a paid locale may only be run for explicitly requested keys; improve, review and rescore take the same keys option.
• Collection – estimate a remote collection by unit id.

Budget modes:
• on_request – cloud runs are refused without keys. dynamic – the monthly budget in [budget] gates the run (ADR-35). The Operations page asks for confirmation before any paid run.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:agent-backlog.title: Operations: agent-backlog
operations:agent-backlog.body:
What it does:
Lists the keys an AI agent (for example Cursor) should still translate, together with the English source text. Output is paste-ready markdown by default. No model is called by this tool.

Which keys appear (reasons):
• missing – no value at all. empty – a blank value. no_state – a value exists but was never recorded (typical after hand edits). stale – the English changed after the translation. external_edit – the value was changed outside the engine after it was recorded.

Options:
• Locales, Namespace and Limit – restrict and cap the list.
• Reasons – a comma-separated subset of the five above.
• Format – prompt (markdown) or json.
• Include existing – shows the current target text on empty, stale and no_state rows so the agent can keep good wording.

Typical loop:
• Run adopt first so hand-edited keys are not reported as missing, paste the backlog into the agent, let it edit the catalogue files, then run adopt again to stamp the new text with agent provenance (ADR-19).

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:agent-hardcoded.title: Operations: agent-hardcoded
operations:agent-hardcoded.body:
What it does:
Finds hardcoded product text in your source code (button labels, messages, titles) and reports it grouped by file for an agent to move into message catalogues. The engine does not rewrite source files and does not invent keys (ADR-32). Nothing is written to your code.

Options:
• Adapter – overrides the configured scanner. Exit 64 with a notice if neither an adapter nor src_dirs is set.
• Limit – cap the number of source files.
• Split – write agent-sized parts (part files plus index.md) instead of one document. Budget tokens and Max hits size each part; Out dir says where they go (ADR-105).
• Format – prompt (paste-ready markdown) or json. The json form carries the stable id and decision of each hit.
• LLM second pass – optional local-model review of the files. Off by default and slow. With Dry run it only lists the files.
• Refresh – rescan even when no file changed. Without it an unchanged tree returns the report stored in the scan cache (ADR-54).
• Submit to taskqueue – a non-dry LLM pass is queued when tq is installed.

Results panel:
• Hits are grouped by confidence: high, medium and low (a member named like its own label, such as SAVE: "Save", is medium). Accept or Ignore each hit, use the bulk buttons for the visible set, or Undo a decision. Show ignored brings hidden hits back.
• What Accept does depends on the apply mode: manual only records the choice, request opens a review ticket on the source locale, auto adds the key and queues its translation (ADR-55).

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:scan-decide.title: Operations: scan-decide
operations:scan-decide.body:
What it does:
Records which scan results are worth localizing. Ids come from the json output of agent-hardcoded. Collection proposals from discover can be decided the same way.

Actions and options:
• Action – accept, ignore, reset (back to pending) or status (counts and the current apply mode; the default).
• Ids – specific hits. Confidence – every pending hit of that level. File – pending hits in files matching a glob. All pending – everything undecided.
• Key – the catalogue key for one accepted hit; refused if that key already holds different text.
• Note and By – stored with the decision for the audit trail.
• Kind – hit (a string in code, the default) or collection.

What accepting does ([apply] mode, ADR-55):
• manual – only records it; run apply afterwards to write the keys.
• request – opens a review ticket on the source locale; closing the ticket adds the key.
• auto – writes the key now and queues its translation.
Ignored hits stay hidden from reports.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:patch.title: Operations: patch
operations:patch.body:
What it does:
Builds a structured changeset and writes patch.json and patch.md. It lists hardcoded strings with a suggested key plus gaps in the catalogues. It changes no catalogue and no source file; use it as a plan to read, review and hand to an agent.

How it behaves:
• Once any scan decision exists, the patch covers only accepted hits. Before any decision it covers everything the scan found.
• Neither patch nor apply edits source code; an agent does that from the report (ADR-32, ADR-55).

Typical order:
• agent-hardcoded to find strings, scan-decide to accept the good ones, patch to review the changeset, apply to write the keys.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:apply.title: Operations: apply
operations:apply.body:
What it does:
Writes the accepted additions into your catalogues. Source-locale keys are created for accepted hardcoded strings, and the source text is copied into each target catalogue as a placeholder so translate can pick the keys up. Source code is never edited.

Options:
• Confirm – required for a real write. Without it nothing is written.
• Dry run – preview exactly what would be added.

Behaviour:
• With scan decisions present, apply covers accepted hits only; otherwise everything proposed. Keys that already hold other text are refused rather than overwritten.
• After applying, run translate (or let the workflow do it) so the placeholders become real translations.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:ingest-visual.title: Operations: ingest-visual
operations:ingest-visual.body:
What it does:
Loads visual QA findings (a JSONL file produced by a Playwright or browse review of your running app) into the review queue. Each finding becomes a ticket on the right locale and key. No model is called (ADR-27).

Options:
• Path – the findings file. The default is the .visual_findings.jsonl next to the context directory, or the [visual] findings_path setting.
• Dry run – parse the file and list the tickets that would be created without writing.

Next steps:
• Open the Review queue to work the tickets, then run validate with Check layout (V28) to confirm that fixed strings fit. The full procedure, including checkpoints and the taskqueue suite, is in docs/visual-findings.md.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:adopt.title: Operations: adopt
operations:adopt.body:
What it does:
Stamps keys that have a catalogue value but no state entry. This happens after someone edits the JSON by hand or with an agent: the engine sees the text but has no record of who wrote it, so it reports the key as missing. Adopt records them with agent provenance (ADR-19). It writes state, scores and history only; catalogue files are not rewritten and stale keys are not refreshed.

Options:
• Locales – default all targets including frozen ones. Namespace – restrict to one. Limit – cap the number stamped.
• Dry run – report without writing.
• Format – text or json.
• Model, Provider and Verified by – override the stamps. Defaults are cursor-agent, agent and cursor-agent.

After running:
• Reload the Dashboard or Editor so overview cards re-read state. The Operations page refreshes the sidecars for you.

Who may run it: Admin only.

operations:sync.title: Operations: sync
operations:sync.body:
What it does:
Gathers work without a background watcher (ADR-1). It runs the scan when configured, counts missing and stale keys, writes proposed_keys.json for hardcoded findings and, unless told not to, submits an incremental translate job.

Options:
• Locales – restrict. Dry run – report only, write nothing and submit nothing.
• No translate – gather the artefacts but do not enqueue translation (sent as submit_translate off).
• Diff – writes work_manifest.json in the state directory listing added, changed and removed keys with the locales that need work.
• Exit non-zero – with Diff, exit 1 when keys were added or changed; a CI gate.
• Strict branch – exit 1 when the checked-out git branch is not the configured source branch (default main).

Cautions:
• Sync warns when it runs on another branch, since pushing source strings from a side branch can delete another branch's translations.
• A real run records each changed English string in source_history.jsonl so the editor can explain why a key is stale.

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:term-report.title: Operations: term-report
operations:term-report.body:
What it does:
Reads the glossary and lists the places where a required term is missing from a translation. It is read-only: nothing is changed and no model is used.

Why it matters:
• The glossary says how product names, domain terms and do-not-translate words must appear. Validation blocks a save that breaks a hard rule, but older translations or imported text can still miss a term. This report finds them so you can fix or requeue them.

Use it with:
• The Glossary page to correct terms, then improve or the editor's Improve to repair affected strings.
• validate, which checks the same terms for the keys you are about to ship.

The command has only the common project, config and branch options.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:release-diff.title: Operations: release-diff
operations:release-diff.body:
What it does:
Compares the current source strings with a snapshot taken earlier by release-freeze and lists what was added, changed or removed since that release. Read-only; no model is used.

Options:
• Name – the release snapshot to compare against (required).

Use it for:
• Release notes for translators: which strings need attention before the next version.
• Checking that a hotfix branch did not alter source text that was already frozen.

Create the snapshot first with release-freeze. The comparison uses source hashes, so a whitespace-only change that alters the text counts as a change.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:release-freeze.title: Operations: release-freeze
operations:release-freeze.body:
What it does:
Takes a named snapshot of the source-string hashes at this moment, for example a release number. The snapshot is stored with the project state and later compared with release-diff.

Options:
• Name – required label for the snapshot.
• Namespaces – optionally limit the snapshot to listed namespaces.
• Keys – optionally limit it to listed keys.

Notes:
• It does not copy translations and does not lock any key; it only remembers what the English looked like. Use the lock action in the editor to protect individual translations.
• Reusing a name is a decision to overwrite that snapshot, so use a new label for each release.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:translate.title: Operations: translate
operations:translate.body:
What it does:
Translates the strings that need it. Only keys that are missing or stale are sent, so adding ten English strings costs roughly ten model calls. Keys already machine, reviewed or human are left alone unless you force it. Translation memory hits are reused without a call (ADR-22).

Options:
• Locales – default every active locale; frozen ones are skipped. Namespace – restrict. Collection – messages by default; file collections use the documents pipeline and remote collections translate each unit from its own source language.
• Model – overrides the configured model for this run. A model change should follow a bakeoff (ADR-12).
• Batch size – keys per request (default 10).
• Force retranslate – also retranslate keys that are up to date. It overwrites machine text.
• Flagged – only keys flagged from the dev overlay.
• Tag – only keys carrying a context tag (set in the editor's Tags field). Several tags mean any of them.
• Pre-translate – stores the text with history trigger pre-translate, with no score row and no low-score flag.
• Ignore min keys – bypasses the [translate] min_keys setting; the Submit button always sets it.
• Dry run – prints the work list and changes nothing.

How it runs:
• Run submits to the taskqueue when it is installed, otherwise runs inline (ADR-28). When the quality model differs from the translation model, scoring is deferred to a second phase so the models do not swap on every key.
• Cloud providers show a cost estimate and ask for confirmation first (ADR-35).

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:improve.title: Operations: improve
operations:improve.body:
What it does:
Retranslates keys with low quality scores, flagged keys and keys marked as needing a better model, using the improve model. The new text is scored and kept only if the score goes up; otherwise the old text stays and history records the rejected attempt.

Options:
• Locales and Namespace – restrict.
• Limit – maximum keys this run (default 50). Dry run – list candidates only.
• Model – overrides the improve model.
• Tag – only keys carrying a context tag, combined with the usual low-score gate.
• Keys – explicit namespace.key entries; skips the low-score gate. Under the on_request cloud budget this is also how a paid locale may be improved.
• Include rejected – retries keys that failed recently. By default those keys rest for a cooldown (default 7 days) so each batch works on different keys.

Notes:
• Human edits are never overwritten. A monthly budget of zero keeps the pass fully local.
• Prefer submitting to the taskqueue for long runs (ADR-28).

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:review.title: Operations: review
operations:review.body:
What it does:
A second pass in which a model reviews existing machine translations. Good ones are promoted from machine to llm_reviewed. A correction is applied only if it passes the same validation as an original translation, so a reviewer that drops a placeholder is not trusted. Rejected strings are marked needs_better_model, the signal to route the language to a larger model.

Options:
• Locales and Namespace – restrict.
• Model – reviewer model; defaults to the locale's translation model.
• Dry run – count what would be reviewed.

Notes:
• Submit to the taskqueue for large runs. Cloud reviewers show a cost estimate and ask for confirmation.
• Do not confuse this with the Review queue page, which holds human review tickets.

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:rescore.title: Operations: rescore
operations:rescore.body:
What it does:
Recomputes quality scores with back-translation, and the LQS judge when one is configured, without changing any translated text. Use it after a scoring rule or model change, to refresh strings you already trust, or to finish scoring after an interrupted deferred translate.

Options:
• Locales and Namespace – restrict.
• Model – overrides the score model (default from [quality] score_model or improve_model).
• Dry run – list the keys that would be rescored; no model call and no writes.

Behaviour:
• Scores are computed in batches (bt_batch_size, default 5) and the worker loads the score model first and stops it afterwards.
• Each run writes a run manifest in the state directory and logs its wall time, which the Progress page uses.
• Submit to the taskqueue for long runs (ADR-28).

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:documents.title: Operations: documents
operations:documents.body:
What it does:
Translates long Markdown documents (terms, privacy policy, help pages) section by section. Only sections whose source changed are retranslated, and the previous translation of a section is shown to the model as a target so wording stays stable.

Options:
• Doc – a single document by file stem, for example terms.
• Doc dir – the document root. Default is content/legal inside the project.
• Locales and Model – as for translate.
• Dry run – show what would be done.

Important:
• If any section fails, the whole locale file is deleted so the page falls back to the source language. A half-translated legal page looks authoritative and is wrong, so the tool prefers no translation.
• Submit to the taskqueue for long documents.

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:bakeoff.title: Operations: bakeoff
operations:bakeoff.body:
What it does:
Translates a fixed set of strings with each candidate model, back-translates them and scores the result. It is the evidence step before choosing a model (ADR-12). It writes a report and a ledger and never changes which model a language uses. Local Ollama models only.

Options:
• Locales – default the first active target. Models – Ollama tags; the locale's current model is always included for comparison. Limit – keys to test, sampled across UI roles (default 30).
• Corpus – a corpus JSON, or the shipped built-in set; default is this project's own strings.
• Out – where REPORT.md, LEDGER.md and matrix_results.jsonl go (default under the state directory).
• Family – prompt family, chat or mt_chat. Matrix – the standard prompt cells. Force cells – re-run cells already in the ledger; by default a retry resumes.
• Dry run – list the cells and call no model.

Reading the result:
• A model passes the gate with a mean back-translation score of at least 0.70 and no glossary-blocking rejects. The Model evaluation page shows the reports. Always compare against the incumbent.

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:export.title: Operations: export
operations:export.body:
What it does:
Produces a handoff file for translators or an agency and downloads it. No model is used.

Options:
• Format – CSV, XLIFF or JSON. Zip is CSV plus screenshots.
• Layout – a single file, or one file per locale or per namespace (delivered as a zip). Files splits the selection into that many files.
• Only – which rows: all, missing, stale, machine, low score and more (untranslated, human, intentional, verified, unverified, unscored, needs_better_model, or a provider).
• Include screenshots – adds the context screenshots and a README, so the download becomes a zip.
• Approved translations only – blanks every translation that is not verified (or reviewed, when [delivery] require says so). The same rule trims the content bundle API.
• Locales and Namespace – restrict. Collection – messages by default.
• Report – also write a JSON report of what was exported.

Round trip:
• Edit the file outside, then bring it back with import. Keep the key columns unchanged.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:import.title: Operations: import
operations:import.body:
What it does:
Reads an exported or translated file back into the catalogues and prints a change report: what was added, changed, skipped or rejected. Imported text is stamped with provider import and goes through the same validation as an editor save.

Form fields:
• File – a CSV, XLIFF 1.2 or 2.0, JSON handoff or zip. The page reads the first file you choose and decides the format from its extension.
• Localized by – the name stamped on imported rows, for example an agency (default import).

CLI options:
• Locales – required for a headerless CSV. Format – only when the name has no suffix. Report – write the JSON report. Dry run – count changes and write nothing.

Cautions:
• A dry run first is wise for files from outside. Rows that fail blocking checks (placeholders, plurals, glossary) are rejected and listed in the report.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:migrate-state.title: Operations: migrate-state
operations:migrate-state.body:
What it does:
Recomputes derived state fields after the structure-signature format changed. Without it every key can look structurally stale, and a policy acting on that could overwrite translations with source text.

When you need it:
• validate reports V08 on a key whose English did not change. That can only mean the stored signature was written by an older or different implementation.

Options:
• Locales – default the active targets. Dry run – report what would change and write nothing.
• Stamp provider – additionally fills a missing provider channel from the model or verifier (ADR-19). This is additive and does not change hashes.

Safety:
• The signature is derived, so nothing needs a model or network. Source hashes, translation dates, models and statuses are untouched, so no translation is invalidated or requeued. Entries whose source key was removed are reported and left alone.

Who may run it: Admin only.

operations:guide.title: Operations: guide
operations:guide.body:
What it does:
A checklist from an empty folder to translations: environment, project, languages, model, optional apply mode, translate, review and ship. It shows how many steps are done and the exact command for the next one. It changes nothing unless you ask for the smoke test.

Options:
• Dir – the folder to inspect when no config exists yet.
• Smoke test – translates one short string with the configured model to confirm it works. A paid cloud provider needs Yes as well.
• Skip provider – do not contact Ollama or any provider, so the page stays quick and offline.
• JSON – machine-readable output. No input – only print the checklist.

Also used by:
• The Getting started card on the Dashboard and the Setup wizard, which show the same steps.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:doctor.title: Operations: doctor
operations:doctor.body:
What it does:
Sanity-checks the installation: Python and package versions, the config, the catalogue paths, whether Ollama answers, and whether the web UI you are using is running current code. Stale web code is the usual reason a recently added button is missing.

Output:
• Each check is ok, warn or fail with a short reason. JSON output is available for scripts.

If the web check fails:
• Stop the old server in its terminal and start llm-localizator web again, then reload the page.

Related:
• Guide reports progress through the workflow; doctor reports the health of the environment.

Who may run it: Admin and Developer.

operations:init.title: Operations: init
operations:init.body:
What it does:
Detects the catalogue layout of a project and writes .llm-localize.toml. Looks in apps/web/messages, src/messages, messages, locales and public/locales.

Options:
• Name – project name (default the directory name). Source locale – default en.
• Format and Path – bypass detection for a new or non-standard layout; both are required together. The path is a template such as static/locales/{locale}.json.
• Taskqueue – also generate blueprint YAML in experiments/operator_queue.
• No register – skip the entry in the project registry.
• Force – overwrite an existing config. Without it an existing config is kept.

Notes:
• Review the written file before translating. The Setup wizard does the same job interactively.

Who may run it: Admin only.

operations:suggest.title: Operations: suggest
operations:suggest.body:
What it does:
Asks the model for one translation of one key and prints it with a score. Nothing is saved: no catalogue value, state, history or translation-memory entry is written. It is what the editor's Suggest button calls.

Options:
• Locale, Namespace and Key – which string to try.
• Alternatives – also ask up to two other configured models (secondary role, roster default) and list their different versions with scores. Skipped for paid cloud projects. In the editor this is the More versions button.
• Ambiguity – also ask which source terms have several senses and which one the translation used. Advice only; it changes no score. Skipped for paid cloud projects. In the editor this is the Flag ambiguous terms checkbox.

Why it exists:
• A Translator cannot run translate, but may ask for a suggestion and then save their own version in the editor, which stamps it as human (ADR-53). Cloud providers may be blocked by the cost ceiling.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Translator.

operations:concordance.title: Operations: concordance
operations:concordance.body:
What it does:
Searches the translation memory for a phrase, showing earlier source and target pairs for the same locale. Read-only and offline.

Options:
• Locale – required. Query – the text to find.
• No source and No target – search only translations or only sources.
• Min similarity – switches to a fuzzy search by word overlap (0.1 to 1; try 0.55) instead of substring.
• Limit – maximum matches. Format – text or json.

Use it to:
• Check how a term was translated before, or find inconsistent wording. The Translation memory page and the editor's TM tab show the same data.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:org.title: Operations: org
operations:org.body:
What it does:
Shows whether this project reads the organisation-level translation memory and glossary that are shared by every project on this machine. Read-only.

Options:
• Format – text or json.

Setup:
• Add [org] use = true to the project config to read the shared memory and glossary after the project's own. contribute = true also writes human-approved text to the shared memory.
• Where the shared files live is set by an org: block in the registry file (tm and glossary); the defaults sit next to it. Use tm-export and glossary-export to reuse them elsewhere.

Notes:
• Lookup order is the project memory, the project's own shared paths, then the organisation. Machine output is never written to the shared memory, only human-approved text, and only when contribute is on.
• The command only reads; it creates no files. File counts of 0 mean nothing has been shared yet.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:tm-export.title: Operations: tm-export
operations:tm-export.body:
What it does:
Writes one locale's translation memory as a TMX file so it can be used in other tools or kept as a backup. Read-only.

Options:
• Locale – required. Out – the file to write; leaving it empty prints to the output.

Notes:
• The Translation memory page also offers an authenticated TMX export. Superseded entries are marked in the file.

Who may run it: every role.

Details:
• The TMX file holds source and target pairs for the chosen locale only, so export each language separately. Entries that were replaced by newer ones are marked superseded.
• Use it to back up the memory before a large tm-import, or to share earlier work with another team or tool. The export reads files only and never calls a model.

operations:tm-import.title: Operations: tm-import
operations:tm-import.body:
What it does:
Merges a TMX file into the translation memory of one locale. Imported units become matches for the next translate run and appear in the editor's TM tab.

Options:
• Locale – required. File – the TMX file.
• Conflict – skip keeps what exists, overwrite-if-higher replaces only with a better score, always replaces.
• Dry run – count the changes and write nothing.

Advice:
• Dry run first. Imported memory is trusted for exact matches, so import only text you have reviewed.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:glossary-export.title: Operations: glossary-export
operations:glossary-export.body:
What it does:
Writes the glossary as CSV or TBX so it can be shared or edited outside. Read-only.

Options:
• Format – csv or tbx. File – the file to write; empty prints to the output.

Notes:
• The domain is not preserved in the export, so keep one file per glossary domain when you re-import.

Who may run it: every role.

Typical uses:
• Send the terms to a translation agency or a terminology tool, back them up, or review them in a spreadsheet. CSV opens in any editor; TBX is the standard interchange format for terminology tools.
• After editing outside, bring the file back with glossary-import, preferably with a dry run first. Terms are injected into every translation prompt, so an exported file with wrong rows can mislead later runs.

operations:glossary-import.title: Operations: glossary-import
operations:glossary-import.body:
What it does:
Merges a CSV or TBX file into the glossary files that are injected into every translation prompt.

Options:
• File and Format – csv or tbx.
• Conflict – skip (default) keeps existing project terms; overwrite replaces them.
• Dry run – parse and write nothing.

Advice:
• Run a dry run and read the counts. After a real import, run term-report and validate to find translations that no longer match the glossary.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:glossary-propose.title: Operations: glossary-propose
operations:glossary-propose.body:
What it does:
Prints candidate glossary terms. Nothing is written to the glossary. With a locale it mines that language's translation memory for short source terms that keep pairing with the same target phrase and are not in the glossary yet.

Options:
• Locale – enables the memory-based mining and gives a CSV in the glossary-import format.
• Min occurrences – how many entries must agree before a term is proposed.
• Out – write the CSV to a file.

Next step:
• Review the CSV, remove wrong rows, then import it with glossary-import.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:impact.title: Operations: impact
operations:impact.body:
What it does:
Lists the locales that became stale because the stored source hash no longer matches the current English. It answers the question what will need retranslation if I ship this source change. Read-only.

Notes:
• A key is stale when its English text or its context fingerprint changed after translation. Follow with estimate-cost to see the price and translate to fix it.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

How to use the result:
• The list is per locale with a count of stale keys, so it shows which languages carry the most work. Run it after merging a branch that changed English text, before you run translate.
• It compares stored hashes only and calls no model, so it is instant and free. Keys that are missing entirely are not stale; status lists those.

operations:pseudo.title: Operations: pseudo
operations:pseudo.body:
What it does:
Writes a throwaway pseudo-locale in which the source text is expanded and accented. It lets you test layouts for longer languages and find hardcoded text without a real translation. It touches neither the state nor the source catalogue.

Options:
• Locale – the code to write the pseudo-locale under.
• Length factor – how much longer the text becomes, for example 1.4.

Notes:
• Delete the generated file when you are done, and never ship it.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:analytics.title: Operations: analytics
operations:analytics.body:
What it does:
Summarizes how quickly runs finished and how long strings wait for scoring or verification. Read-only; it reads the run manifests the pipeline writes.

Options:
• Run command – translate, improve, review or rescore. Locale and Locales – restrict. Model – filter by model. Since – a start date. Last – only the most recent N runs. Format – text or json.

Lag report:
• The median hours from translation to score and to verification, and how many keys still carry only a heuristic score.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:metrics.title: Operations: metrics
operations:metrics.body:
What it does:
Process metrics from the history files: how many strings a machine translated, how many of those a person then edited, the edit rate, the mean hours until the first human edit, and coverage with a weekly trend. No model is used.

Options:
• Locale – restrict. Since – 30d, 12h, 2w or a date. Why low – group keys scored below Threshold by their weakest quality dimension (placeholders, terminology, fluency …); keys without stored dimensions show as no-dimensions and unscored keys are not counted. The model and prompt rule are not recorded, so they are not named. By – user, locale or locale+user switches to the activity report: edits counted per translator and/or locale. Format – text, json or csv (csv needs By).

Notes:
• Cells that start with = + - or @ are prefixed with a quote so spreadsheets do not run them as formulas.
• History retention limits how far back the figures go, and the coverage trend is approximate. The Dashboard and Progress pages show the same data.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:flag-source.title: Operations: flag-source
operations:flag-source.body:
What it does:
Flags an English string as unclear or wrong. The flag is a review ticket on the source locale, so it never triggers a retranslation. Use it when a translator cannot translate a string because the English is ambiguous.

Options:
• Namespace and Key – the string. Note – the reason, for example whether a word is a verb or a noun.

Next step:
• See source-review-queue for the open flags. The editor offers the same action as Flag English.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:source-review-queue.title: Operations: source-review-queue
operations:source-review-queue.body:
What it does:
Lists the English strings that people flagged for review and that are still open. Read-only.

Notes:
• The Dashboard shows the same list as English flagged for review. Resolve the ticket in the Review queue once the English text has been fixed.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

Working the flags:
• Each row shows the key, the English text and the note left by whoever flagged it. Fix the English in your source catalogue, then resolve the ticket in the Review queue page.
• Changing the English makes the translations stale, so run impact and then translate afterwards. Flags never change any translation by themselves.

operations:task.title: Operations: task
operations:task.body:
What it does:
Lists, creates and deletes tasks: named sets of keys with one assignee per locale and an optional due date.

Options:
• Action – list, create or delete.
• Name, Namespace or Keys, Assign (locale=person) and Due – what to create.
• Unverified – keep only keys not yet verified in an assigned locale.
• Assignee – list only one person's tasks.

Notes:
• A task holds no text; progress counts verified keys per locale.
• Overdue tasks are marked in the list. Nothing is sent outside the app.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Translator.

operations:discuss.title: Operations: discuss
operations:discuss.body:
What it does:
Keeps a discussion thread per key: questions about the English or the translation, with @mentions and a resolved state.

Options:
• Action – list, add, resolve or reopen.
• Namespace and Key – the key the thread belongs to.
• Text – the comment; write @name to mention a person.
• Open only and Mention – narrow the list.

Notes:
• A thread is shared by every language and holds no translation text.
• A new comment on a resolved thread reopens it. Nothing is sent outside the app.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:draft.title: Operations: draft
operations:draft.body:
What it does:
Keeps a model suggestion as a draft until a person accepts it. Nothing is written to the catalogue before then.

Options:
• Action – list, create, accept or reject.
• Locale, Namespace and Key – the key to draft; accept and reject also take Keys (namespace.key).

Notes:
• Create stores the text with the English it was made from; a draft whose English has changed is shown as stale and cannot be accepted.
• Mode minimal-edit (create only) asks the model to edit the existing translation as little as possible after a recorded source change, instead of translating again. It is opt-in, obeys the cloud gate, and still lands as a draft for review.
• Accept validates the text and writes it as a human edit recorded in history as draft-accept; locked and verified keys are skipped.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Translator.

operations:open-pr.title: Operations: open-pr
operations:open-pr.body:
What it does:
Sends the catalogue files you changed to your git host as a pull request. Plan shows what would be sent and writes nothing; open creates a branch, commits those files, pushes it and opens the pull request; status checks one branch once.

Options:
• Action – plan, open or status.
• Branch – status only: the pull request branch to check.
• Confirm – open only: required, because it pushes a branch.

Setup:
• Add [git_host] enabled = true to the project config. Optional settings are remote, base and branch_prefix. GitHub is used through the gh command, which must already be signed in.

Notes:
• Only changed files under the catalogue folder are staged, by path; other changes in the working tree are left alone.
• The commit message and pull request text end with Co-authored-by lines for the editors and models recorded in history since the base branch's last commit.
• Nothing polls: status asks the host once per request.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:screenshot-link.title: Operations: screenshot-link
operations:screenshot-link.body:
What it does:
Attaches a screenshot to a string so translators see the screen it appears on. A link can outline one region of the image.

Options:
• Action – list, link or unlink.
• File – the image path inside the project's screenshots folder (png, jpg or webp).
• Namespace and key – the string the image belongs to.
• Region – x, y, width and height as fractions of the image, between 0 and 1.
• Note – an optional short caption.

Notes:
• Linking the same image, key and region twice keeps one link.
• Visual findings that name a key and a screenshot are linked automatically when ingested.
• Links are only reference material; they never change translations or prompts.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:source-diff.title: Operations: source-diff
operations:source-diff.body:
What it does:
For one key, shows how its English source changed: the old and new text, the current translation, and the words of the new text that the old translation does not cover yet. Read-only.

Options:
• Namespace and Key – the string to inspect.
• Locale – also show that locale's current translation.
• Format – text or json.

Notes:
• The change comes from the source-change log, which sync fills in when an English string is edited. A key with no recorded change reports that and nothing else.
• The json result lists the difference as spans (equal, insert, delete, replace) plus the new text split into spans flagged as needing translation, so the editor can colour them.
• To get an updated translation without retranslating, run draft create with mode minimal-edit; the result waits as a draft and is never applied on its own.

Who may run it: every role.

operations:find-replace.title: Operations: find-replace
operations:find-replace.body:
What it does:
Finds text in one locale's translations and shows each key before and after, so you can fix a term everywhere.

Options:
• Locale – the language to change.
• Find and Replace – literal text; matching ignores case unless Case sensitive is on.
• Namespace – limit to one file.
• Keys – the keys to change; without them, and without Confirm, the op only lists matches.

Notes:
• Each result is checked by the validator; verified and locked keys are skipped and shown with the reason.
• Writes are stamped as human edits and recorded in history as find-replace.

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:apply-near.title: Operations: apply-near
operations:apply-near.body:
What it does:
Copies the saved translation of one key onto similar keys you tick. Identical English texts are already filled when you save; this covers near matches.

Options:
• Locale, Namespace and Key – the key whose translation is copied.
• Min similarity – smallest likeness of the English texts, 0 to 1 (default 0.85).
• Keys – the targets to write; without them, and without Confirm, the op only lists candidates.

Notes:
• Each target is checked by the validator; verified, locked, human-edited and intentional keys are skipped and shown with the reason.
• Writes are stamped as human edits and recorded in history as apply-near.

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:bulk-clear.title: Operations: bulk-clear
operations:bulk-clear.body:
What it does:
Sends keys back to the translate backlog by dropping their state entry. The old text stays in the catalogue as a fallback until a new translation replaces it. Human, verified and locked keys are always kept.

Options:
• Locale – required. Stale to source – picks keys whose English changed. Purge machine older than – picks machine translations older than the given number of days.
• Invalid – picks translations that fail a hard check (a stray backslash, foreign script, placeholder or HTML mismatch). Latin leftover – picks non-Latin translations that contain Latin words the source does not.
• Confirm – required for a real change; without it the command only lists what it would clear. Dry run – list only.

Notes:
• A row stamped human whose provider is import or agent counts as a hand-off copy and can be cleared; a real web edit cannot (ADR-48, ADR-57).

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:rename-placeholder.title: Operations: rename-placeholder
operations:rename-placeholder.body:
What it does:
Renames a placeholder (for example {name} to {user}) in the English text and in every translation, so translations are not marked stale. It handles {x, number}, the variable of plural/select and placeholders inside branches; %s and {{x}} are not touched.

Options:
• Old name and New name – required, word characters only.
• Namespace and Keys – restrict the change.
• Confirm – required for a real change; without it (or with Dry run) it only lists what would change.

Notes:
• Keys whose English already uses the new name are skipped.
• Translation memory is not rewritten.
• Provenance stays: a human edit stays human (ADR-48).

Who may run it: Admin and Supervisor.

operations:hard-keys.title: Operations: hard-keys
operations:hard-keys.body:
What it does:
Compares quality scores across languages to find keys that are hard in every language, which usually means the English is ambiguous, from keys that are hard only in one language, which usually means a model problem. No model is called.

Options:
• Locales and Namespace – restrict.
• Threshold – score below which a locale counts as low (default 0.7).
• Min locales – minimum number of locales with a score for a key (default 4).
• Format – text or json. Dry run – report only and do not write the report file.

Use it to:
• Decide which English strings to rewrite or flag, and which languages need a different model.

Who may run it: Admin, Supervisor and Developer.

operations:explain-scan.title: Opérations : explain-scan
operations:explain-scan.body:
Ce que ça fait :
Explique pourquoi le détecteur de textes codés en dur a signalé ou non une ligne de votre code source. Il rejoue l’analyse de ce fichier et montre chaque étape : si le fichier est sous [scan] src_dirs, ignoré comme documentation ou test ou par [scan] exclude, quel analyseur le lit, et chaque résultat de la ligne avec son niveau et sa raison. Le texte non signalé reçoit le premier filtre qui l’a écarté : dans un appel de traduction, un jeton d’API ou d’énumération, pas de la prose, ou aucune règle pour cette position.

Options :
• Fichier – chemin relatif à la racine du projet. Ligne – facultative ; sans elle, tous les résultats du fichier sont listés.
• Adaptateur – remplace l’analyseur configuré.

À quoi ça sert :
• Choisir entre corriger le code, ajouter une directive d’ignorance ou signaler une lacune de l’analyseur.

Rien n’est écrit. Qui peut l’exécuter : tout le monde.

operations:acknowledge-flush.title: Operations: acknowledge-flush
operations:acknowledge-flush.body:
What it does:
Deletes an interrupted flush journal without writing catalogues. A flush journal is left behind when a run was stopped while writing; the next run refuses to start until it is resolved.

When to use it:
• Only after you checked that the catalogue files are in the state you want, for example after restoring from version control. Using it discards the record of what was being written.

Who may run it: Admin only.

How to decide:
• Look at the Progress page and the catalogue files in version control. If they match what you expect, acknowledging is safe. If you are unsure, restore the files from git first.
• The command has no options and only deletes the journal file; it never rewrites catalogue or state files, and it does not retry the interrupted run. After it, run status to see what is still missing and start the run again.
